questions.question: Describe how the base, mast and arm are made from the working drawing, including how card is stiffened and how a lattice mast is made rigid, and how the mast is tested.
questions.expected_answer: With the flow chart open the base is made first: an A4 outline marked on double card from the drawing's dimensions, cut on the mat with the knife against a ruler and blade away from the body, the two layers glued to the edges and pressed flat under a book, with the mast position marked at 100 millimetres from the front edge and central before the glue sets. The mast is 350 millimetres of card rolled tightly round a pencil to 20 millimetres diameter, glued and taped, a tube resisting bending far better than flat card; a lattice alternative uses four skewers at the corners of a 20 millimetre square glued to card rungs at base, middle and top with a diagonal or gusset on every face so no face remains a parallelogram. The mast is tested by holding the base and pushing the top sideways both ways without sway. The arm is a 250 millimetre tube or a folded triangular section made stiff first, with a tie string cut if drawn, and the winch and pulley are made while the glue dries.

questions.question: Explain how the winch and tip pulley are made and how the crane is assembled and wired in the order of the flow chart, with the tool rules followed.
questions.expected_answer: The winch is a cotton reel glued on a skewer so it cannot spin, with a handle fixed at right angles 75 millimetres from the axle through two holes in double card glued both sides or as a bound wire with a card tube grip, two card cheeks with holes slightly larger than the skewer, a bead between cheek and drum to prevent rubbing, and a notch and peg that the handle rests against so the load cannot run back. The tip pulley is a bead or grooved card disc on a straightened paper clip through the arm 10 millimetres from the end, with card cheeks either side, the wire ends bent and taped along the arm, spinning freely. Assembly: mast glued upright on the pencil cross with four gussets, arm fitted to the mast top with a card sleeve or gussets and the tie string pulled level, winch cheeks glued at the mast foot so the drum sits directly below the mast, string tied to the drum and run up through a guide at the mast top, along the arm, over the pulley and tied to the magnet's loop, cell holder and switch taped at the back edge, leads run down and the loop wired as on the circuit diagram, switch pressed to check the indicator. Scissors for single card, knife on the mat for double card and tubes, thin glue clamped while drying, hot glue only at the teacher's station, bench kept clear of offcuts.

questions.question: Describe the whole-crane test, what is recorded, the fix for each common failure, and how the model is finished.
questions.expected_answer: A dish of mixed clips, foil balls, a copper coin and a brass screw is placed under the arm's tip and a bin marked 200 millimetres to the side. With the switch pressed the magnet is lowered by the crank into the pile and wound up, the height above the base read with a ruler at the top of the lift against the 150 millimetre requirement, the arm swung or tipped to the bin, the switch released and the load watched to drop with the indicator going out; only steel clips should have crossed, and the base's back edge must not lift. Three repeats are recorded against each specification: clips lifted, height, distance, release time, non-ferrous carried, tipping, bulb on with magnet. Fixes one at a time with retests: a bending arm gets a tie or second tube, tipping is cured by moving the cells back, adding permitted weight or shortening the arm, a winch that runs back gets a better stop peg, a derailing string gets a deeper groove or cheek, a twisting magnet gets a paper-clip swivel. When passed, loose string is trimmed and taped, the base labelled with team and project, the flow chart's last box ticked, the crane sketched or photographed and delays noted for the evaluation.
